one_liner: Header-only bump/arena allocator for same-lifetime objects; 5.4x faster than glibc new/delete when a whole batch is freed at once.
what_it_does: fastcpp::arena hands out memory from cache-line-aligned blocks (64 KiB by default, configurable, minimum 1 KiB) and never frees a single object: reset() rewinds to empty but keeps the blocks for the next round, and release() or the destructor returns them. It does not look like new/delete. a.create<T>(args...) placement-constructs a trivially destructible T, create_array<T>(n) returns a std::span over uninitialized storage, copy() interns a byte range, and arena_allocator<T> lets std containers use it, with a deallocate that does nothing. It is one header in the fastcpp catalogue repo (developer source), next to a benchmark and a write-up (docs/allocators.md) arguing that most programs do not need an allocator library.
how_it_is_fast: It is bump-pointer (region) allocation. The force-inlined fast path aligns the cursor, checks it against the block end and moves it forward. There is no size-class lookup, per-object header or free list, and running out of a block goes to a separate noinline slow path. Freeing n objects is one O(1) cursor reset instead of n delete calls, and blocks kept across reset() are reused without calling operator new again. Consecutive allocations sit next to each other in order, which is why a linked list built in the arena walked 4.75x faster than one that glibc malloc spread out between other allocations.
when_to_use: Build-then-drop batches of many small, trivially destructible objects that die together: AST/IR nodes for one file, per-frame renderer scratch, one parse or one request. Measured: 200k 48-byte nodes allocated, filled and freed at 5.41x the speed of glibc new/delete.

Repeated cycles of the same shape (per frame, per request): reset() keeps every block, so steady-state rounds make no further operator new calls. A unit test checks that bytes_reserved() and block_count() stay constant across reset().

Pointer-linked structures (lists, trees, graphs) that are walked long after they are built, on glibc malloc: contiguous placement made a post-build list walk 4.75x faster than a heap fragmented by interleaved allocations.
Interning strings or byte ranges that live as long as the batch, via copy().
Backing a std::vector or another std container in code you do not own, via arena_allocator<T>, when its contents can be dropped with the arena and its final size can be reserved up front.
when_not_to_use: Objects freed in an order unrelated to their creation (caches, pools, graphs with deletions): no single object can be freed, so memory only grows until reset(). For this churn case the repo's own measurement says to swap malloc instead, e.g. LD_PRELOAD jemalloc at 2.71x over glibc new/delete.
Types with non-trivial destructors (std::string, containers, RAII handles): create<T> and create_array<T> reject them with a static_assert because the arena never runs destructors.

When std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource is acceptable. It has been in the standard since C++17 and was only about 25% slower (4.32 vs 3.45 ns/node) on the same bulk workload. The repo's own doc says to reach for a bump pointer, not a dependency.
Allocating from one arena on several threads: the class has no locking or atomics, and thread safety is not documented.

When allocation is a small share of runtime: the doc's own Amdahl table puts the saving from a 5x arena at 0.8% of runtime when allocation is 1% of it. It is also an immature component: arena.hpp is from a single 2026-09-02 commit (author 'Claude'), has 5 unit tests, and sits in a private repo with 0 stars and no issue history.

integration.dependencies: none beyond the standard library and the repo's own include/fastcpp/core/bits.hpp and core/macros.hpp (3 headers, ~550 lines). The CMake target fastcpp::fastcpp, however, links all ten vendored third-party libraries (simdjson, yyjson and CRoaring are compiled static libs, the last two in C) and requests cxx_std_23, so copy the three headers rather than using add_subdirectory if you only want the arena.
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 (std::span, <bit>, std::is_constant_evaluated). The arena was benchmarked with gcc 13.3 at -std=c++20. The repo as a whole now targets C++23 and lists gcc 13+, clang 17+ or MSVC 19.35+, with CMake 3.20+.
integration.platforms: any. The arena has no ISA-specific code. CI builds on Linux (gcc, clang) and macOS (clang), and core/macros.hpp has MSVC branches, but MSVC is not in CI. Performance numbers exist only for x86-64 Linux.
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the class holds plain cursor/end pointers with no synchronization, so use one arena per thread
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it does not replace new/delete. You call a.create<T>(...) and never delete, and objects must be trivially destructible. arena_allocator<T> is a std::allocator-compatible adapter for std containers, but its deallocate is a no-op.

gotchas: Lifetime is manual and unchecked: reset(), release() or destroying the arena while a pointer or an arena_allocator-backed container still refers to its memory leaves dangling pointers, and there is no diagnostic. arena_allocator also skips the trivially-destructible check that create<T> enforces.
arena_allocator::deallocate does nothing, so a std::vector grown with push_back leaves every outgrown buffer in the arena until reset(). Call reserve() first.

Waste in the slow path: a request larger than the block size gets its own block of next_pow2(bytes + alignment), so allocate(1 MiB) reserves 2 MiB. Moving to a new block abandons the tail of the current one. After reset(), a request too big for the next kept block walks past and strands each such block until the next reset().

alignment must be a power of two, and nothing checks it (align_up is mask arithmetic). create_array<T> returns uninitialized storage. allocate() is not noexcept: a new block comes from aligned ::operator new, which can throw std::bad_alloc.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No siblings catalogued yet. Against the standard library's own arena, std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource, it measured 3.45 vs 4.32 ns/node (about 1.25x) in the same suite, so pick it only when that margin matters more than using a standard type.
verified_claims_summary: On a shared 4-core Intel Xeon 2.10GHz VM (Ubuntu 24.04, gcc 13.3, -O2 -march=native, libstdc++ and glibc malloc), allocating, filling and freeing 200k 48-byte nodes took 3.45 ns/node with the arena vs 18.68 ns with new/delete (5.41x), and walking the resulting list afterwards took 2.74 vs 13.03 ns (4.75x). Under LD_PRELOAD jemalloc, new/delete only improves to 12.63 ns on the bulk case, but the walk gap shrinks to about 1.45x. These are first-party minimum-of-samples numbers: the recorded run commit predates bench_allocator.cpp, and HEAD now builds benchmarks at -O3.
status_note: The repo (private:developer-source) is PRIVATE, readable only with granted access, and has 0 stars. arena.hpp has not changed since its single 2026-09-02 commit, and the repo was last pushed 2026-09-04. It is MIT-licensed and small enough to copy: 247 lines plus two core headers. CI at HEAD is red for unrelated reasons (an xsimd bench build and a UBSan hit in string/parse.hpp), but test_containers, which holds the arena tests, passes under ASan+UBSan.
